analysis.one_liner: Requires phone companies to verify callers and offer free robocall-blocking technology to customers.
analysis.headline: The House subcommittee held one hearing in April 2019, and the bill never reached the full Energy and Commerce Committee or the House floor before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required phone and text messaging companies, at no extra charge, to verify that caller ID information is accurate and to give customers technology that blocks automated robocalls and texts. It also would have made it illegal to interfere with call-blocking tools and let consumers sue providers that failed to offer them. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone: the bill's findings cite nearly 5.8 million unwanted-call complaints to the FTC in fiscal 2018, note that scammers especially target the elderly, and cite an estimated $350 million lost to telemarketing fraud in 2011. Consumers would have gotten free caller-ID verification and blocking tools instead of paying extra for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone customers, especially older adults targeted by scams

how_it_helps.text: Requires originating providers to enable, at no additional charge, technology that verifies a caller's ID accurately identifies them, with unverified calls flagged or blocked [S3].

Requires receiving providers, at no additional charge, to offer customers tools that block unverified calls and block automated dialer calls unless the customer consented or the call is from a public-safety entity [S3].

Makes it unlawful to interfere with call-blocking technology, and gives state attorneys general and private consumers legal claims — including $500 per violation — against providers that fail to offer the required technology [S3].
Requires the FCC to report to Congress every four years on whether the standards actually reduced unwanted calls, with reports posted on a public website [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telephone and text messaging providers, which would have to build and run verification and blocking technology 'for no additional charge.' Legitimate high-volume callers (such as appointment reminders or emergency notifications) would have to go through an FCC vetting process to be whitelisted. Some compliance costs could eventually show up in phone bills.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates carriers provide the technology at no additional charge, so companies bear the cost of building and operating verification and blocking systems; over time those costs can be recovered through rates [S3].

Automated blocking risks catching legitimate calls: the bill itself builds an appeals process and an FCC-vetted 'whitelisting' system for essential-services callers such as domestic violence shelters and medical practices, an acknowledgment that over-blocking is a real problem [S3].

Requiring subscribers to use caller-ID verification technology could create administrative burdens for small businesses and legitimate callers who need to mask their numbers, though the bill preserves a 'Caller ID Blocked' option and an exemption process for legitimate needs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers — fewer scam calls reaching vulnerable people, free blocking instead of paid add-ons — is substantial and the bill includes careful safeguards (exemptions, appeals, whitelisting) against over-blocking. The main cost falls on providers as an unfunded mandate, and some of it could be passed back to customers, but the design is targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, which held one hearing, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the ROBOCOP Act in the House on April 12, 2019 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and, three days later, to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on April 30, 2019 — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill attracted 20 cosponsors, all House Democrats, but never received a markup or a vote in the full committee or on the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telephone and wireless carriers, which avoided a mandate to provide call-verification and blocking technology at no charge, and high-volume callers who would otherwise have faced FCC vetting to reach customers. Phone customers continued to bear unwanted calls and pay for blocking features.

industries.note: The bill would have required providers to build caller-ID verification and offer blocking tools 'for no additional charge,' an unfunded compliance cost. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against customers who would have received the technology free instead of as a paid add-on.

Verified caller ID and default blocking of unverified and autodialed calls would have cut off the main channel for scam and unwanted calls. The bill's own findings blame illegitimate operators and foreign-originated calls for evading the do-not-call registry.
Requiring carriers to provide blocking technology to subscribers at no additional charge would have competed with premium third-party blocking services customers currently pay for.
